articles.title: Brickbat: Listening In
articles.content:
Dylan Hembrough, editor in chief of the student newspaper at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, contacted the school's communications office to protest a policy requiring a communications staff member to sit in on interviews between student reporters and university staff. As a result, university officials reported Hembrough to campus police for harassment. Police looked into the report, decided his comments did not constitute harassment, and recommended dropping the case. In a statement, the communications office defended the policy and said the real problem is that the student paper has printed inaccurate information and refused to retract it.

The post Brickbat: Listening In appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Fusionism and its Limits
articles.content:
Recent political developments have rekindled longstanding debates over "fusionism," the combination of libertarianism and conservative traditionalism that dominated the American right from roughly the late 1970s through the early years of this century. That dominance has been severely undermined and likely overthrown by the rise of nationalism and "postliberalism." But some would like to revive it. Reason editor Stephanie Slade's important new book Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right outlines one notable case for such a revival.
I agree with Slade, Jonathan Adler, and others that fusionism is far preferable to nationalism and postliberalism. But I am skeptical about its political viability. In addition, fusionism has significant conceptual flaws. Finally, at least in the short to medium term future, an alliance with "abundance liberals" is probably a more promising political strategy for libertarians than a revival of fusionism.
Despite my relative skepticism about a revival, I readily acknowledge fusionism's significant past achievements, and ongoing superiority over various other tendencies on the conservative right. Between the 1970s and the early 2000s, fusionist conservatives and libertarians (sometimes with the help of moderate/"neoliberal" Democrats) made huge contributions to such achievements as deregulation of many sectors of the economy, reducing tax rates, reinvigorating constitutional protection for property rights and limits on federal government power, and the West's triumph in the Cold War. While early fusionists sometimes undervalued the Civil Rights movement and were soft on racism, over time most of them came to promote color-blindness and and abjuring racial and ethnic discrimination in government policy. They even, for a long time, succeeded in making racial and ethnic color-blindness the dominant approach to such issues in the conservative movement. William F. Buckley and other fusionists also worked to purge the political right of its longstanding tendencies towards anti-Semitism. In combination, these are no small achievements.
The Rise of Right-Wing Nationalism and Postliberalism
But, especially over the last decade, fusionism has been displaced by nationalism as the dominant ideology of the Republican Party and the conservative movement. Where fusionism sought to reconcile traditionalism and liberty, nationalism is a grave menace to liberty across a wide range of issues. Consider Donald Trump's massive tariffs, federal takeovers of numerous private corporations, attempts to use the FCC and other government agencies to undermine free speech, and policy of mass deportations (which threatens the civil liberties and economic future of native-born citizens as well as immigrants).
Instead of color-blindness and nondiscrimination, we now have a conservative movement increasingly permeated with racial and ethnic bigotry and anti-Semitism of the kind fusionists sought to purge. Prominent right-wing "influencers" go so far as to claim we need to bar Indian immigrants because they work too hard and undermine the objectives of "homogeneity" and "maintain[ing] a white majority in the country." Many congressional Republicans also promote religious discrimination in immigration and other policies. In foreign policy, Trump has undermined relations with liberal democratic allies like Canada, Australia, and the nations of the European Union, and kowtowed towards illiberal nationalist authoritarians like Vladimir Putin.
Trump's idiosyncratic personal predilections contribute to some of these developments. But most arise from inherent tendencies of nationalism, which gravitates towards a zero-sum view of the world that leads to expanded government control of the economy, repression of racial and ethnic minorities, undermining civil liberties, and authoritarianism.
The "postliberalism" advocated by many leading right-wing intellectuals and activists is just as bad. Postliberals like Adrian Vermeule and Patrick Deneen are very clear about their desire to massively expand government control over the economy and civil society, and destroy both economic and personal liberties. Unlike nationalism, postliberalism has little mass public support. But it does have considerable influence among the intellectuals and activists who may staff future Republican administrations and congressional offices.
Illiberal big-government nationalism holds a strong sway over the Republican base. The 2024 election dramatically illustrates that. In the 2024 GOP presidential primary, Trump was challenged by Nikki Haley (a prominent advocate of traditional fusionism) and Ron DeSantis (popular governor of a major red state who tried to, in effect, split the difference between MAGA nationalism and pre-2016 conservatism). And, yet, despite the events of January 6, 2021 and numerous scandals, Trump not only beat these opponents, but did so very easily. While that was partly due to his particular type of charisma, it also highlights the influence of illiberal nationalism over the GOP. Even now, with Trump increasingly unpopular, most congressional Republicans shy away from challenging his worst policies, for fear of losing to MAGA types in GOP primaries. Many of those who are willing to challenge him on major issues have either been ousted in GOP primaries (like Rep. Thomas Massie), or chose not to run for reelection because of the likelihood of suffering that fate (e.g. - Rep. Don Bacon).
Facing a difficult political environment in the 2026 midterm elections, some congressional Republicans have become more willing to criticize a few of Trump's policies, such as the badly mismanaged Iran War. But very few have repudiated his big-government nationalism across the board or called for a return to fusionism.
Perhaps this will all change once Trump leaves the scene. But we shouldn't count on it. At this point, the major likely contenders for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination - Vice-President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio - seem like they are vying for the mantle of inheritors of Trump's worst tendencies, not opponents of them.
Inherent Limitations of Fusionism
Even if fusionists do manage to regain control of the Republican Party and the conservative movement, the ideology's inherent limitations might undermine its value. The extent to which fusionism is compatible with strong protections for economic and personal liberty is actually ambiguous. Frank Meyer, a key founder of fusionism in the 1950s and 60s, famously argued that liberty and virtue are mutually reinforcing because liberty is what enables people to be truly virtuous. A person who only does the right thing because he is forced to by the state isn't truly virtuous at all. Think, for example, of a man who only refrains from violence and theft for fear of going to prison. A paragon of virtue he is not.
This position has considerable merit. But most social conservatives, including many otherwise sympathetic to fusionism, don't fully buy it, or even come close. They argue that, at least in many instances, we want to achieve virtuous behavior, regardless of the motivation for it. Or, at least, that doing the right thing for a bad reason is far preferable to not doing it at all. Thus, if you believe that using pornography, prostitution, gambling, taking various drugs, and so on are inherently immoral, then you may well advocate using government power to suppress these activities, even if people who only refrain out of fear of punishment are not as virtuous as those who abjure them voluntarily.
Many conservative fusionists do, in fact, believe that a wide range of consensual activities like the above are inherently evil. Alternatively, many believe that we have to suppress at least some of them out of paternalism. For example, they argue we must suppress drugs, prostitution, and gambling, because people who do these things don't understand what's good for them.
For these reasons, most conservative fusionists have in fact been willing to endorse many policies that severely curtail liberty. Even Ronald Reagan - the president whose administration most exemplified fusionism - promoted a major expansion of the War on Drugs, a federal policy that massively curtails liberty by killing or imprisoning hundreds of thousands people merely because they have used, possessed, or distributed substances the government considers too risky. Reagan's drug policies were not as bad as Trump's policy of outright murdering supposed drug dealers in the Caribbean and Pacific. But they were very bad, even so - and a striking example of the limitations of fusionism.
Elsewhere, I have argued that, at this moment in political history, the best available potential allies for libertarians are "abundance liberals." They are by no means perfect. But they agree with us - to a large extent - on numerous major issues, including trade, immigration, nuclear power, "YIMBY" housing deregulation, and more. And, like us, they tend to oppose both left and right-wing ethnic identity politics (on which latter point see recent articles by Matt Yglesias and Kelsey Piper). On the whole, they are less paternalistic and less prone to advocate suppression of consensual activities than most fusionist conservatives. They also have considerably greater influence over the Democratic Party and the political left, generally, than fusionists currently have in the Republican Party and the conservative movement.
The left, of course, has its own dangerous illiberal menace in the form of "democratic socialists," whose statism has much in common with that of MAGA nationalists. But this faction is nowhere near dominating the Democratic Party and the political left to the degree that nationalists have come to dominate the right.
None of this proves that libertarians cannot continue work with fusionist conservatives at all. There are many issues on which there is still room for cooperation. I myself have worked with such conservatives in the Society for the Rule of Law, and in the effort to combat Trump's tariffs (where they played crucial roles in the litigation that led to the invalidation of Trump's IEEPA tariff power grab by the Supreme Court and in currently ongoing efforts to challenge his attempts to use other laws to reimpose sweeping tariffs). Some conservative fusionists are more pro-liberty than others. And, for most, there is considerable variation across issues.
And, perhaps, things will be different in a decade or two. The Trumpist moment in right-wing politics may dissipate over time, though it seems unlikely to do so quickly.
Productive cooperation between libertarians and (some) conservatives is still very much possible. But we should recognize that fusionists are unlikely to regain control over the conservative movement anytime soon, and that fusionism has notable inherent limitations. Thus, we should look for other allies, and carefully limit the percentage of our eggs that we put in the fusionist basket. At this point, it cannot safely hold very many of them.
The post Fusionism and its Limits appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Kansas Ban on Private Parties' Partially Prefilling Voters' Mail Ballot Applications Upheld
articles.content:
A short excerpt from today's longish Tenth Circuit opinion in VoteAmerica v. Schwab, by Judge Timothy Tymkovich, joined by Judges Michael Murphy and Joel Carson:
To reduce voter confusion and increase confidence in elections, the Kansas legislature prohibited private parties from partially prefilling applications for mail ballots before those applications are sent to registered voters. VoteAmerica and Voter Participation Center sued, alleging that the restriction infringed on their freedom of speech guaranteed by the First Amendment….
Relying on the political reaction against mail-in voting and Kansas's failure to prove an adequate fit between its stated interests and the Prohibition, the [district] court concluded that Kansas enacted the Prohibition to suppress speech supporting mail-in voting. Applying strict scrutiny (and intermediate scrutiny in the alternative), the court concluded that the law failed because it was not sufficiently tailored….
[W]e REVERSE the district court's judgment. The district court found an improper purpose without evidence from the Prohibition's justifications, text, or legislative history; it instead inferred an improper purpose from the national political debate on mail-in voting. That finding was in error. Because the Prohibition was enacted without an improper purpose, we apply intermediate scrutiny and find the Prohibition constitutional….
The court held the law was viewpoint-neutral (and content-neutral):
VPC [plaintiff Voter Participation Center] bears the burden to show that the Prohibition was enacted with viewpoint-discriminatory purpose…. A law is adopted with improper purpose if it was adopted "because of disagreement with the message the speech conveys." …
We do not, however, assume that a law is adopted with improper purpose simply "because it may disproportionately affect speech on certain topics," or because "it has an incidental effect on some speakers or messages but not others." McCullen v. Coakley (2014)….
Kansas contends that the district court wrongly inferred improper purpose when the Prohibition's text, enactment history, and the State's justifications for the law evince no such purpose. We agree.
First, Kansas's stated interests in the Prohibition are not intrinsically tied to restricting a viewpoint. Kansas stated that the Prohibition is meant to (1) minimize voter confusion; (2) facilitate efficiency in election administration; and (3) foster confidence in and protect the integrity of the electoral process. These are each legitimate interests—and they are independent of any alleged purpose in restricting VPC's pro-mail-in-voting viewpoint….
VPC counters that we must look beyond Kansas's stated interests to the Prohibition's operation. For, if "[e]very objective indication shows that the provision's primary purpose is to restrict speech that [advances a certain viewpoint]," we should not conclude that the provision was enacted with a proper purpose "simply because the statute itself and those defending it in court say that it is[.]" See McCullen (Scalia, J., concurring). VPC highlights the Prohibition's disproportionate effect on the pro-mail-in-voting viewpoint. It urges that the Prohibition functions to target only mail-in voting advocates because those against mail-in voting would not prefill applications.
That may be true, but caselaw forecloses VPC's argument. Without more, incidental disproportionate effect on one subject or viewpoint does not prove improper purpose. See McCullen (majority opinion) ("[A] facially neutral law does not become content based simply because it may disproportionately affect speech on certain topics.")….
VPC fails to show that Kansas enacted the Prohibition to suppress its pro-mail-voting viewpoint. The district court's reliance on cultural antagonism against mail-in voting to infer the Kansas legislature enacted the prohibition with an improper purpose—when the law's justifications, text, and enactment history reveal no such purpose—was in error….
And the court held that the law passed the intermediate scrutiny applicable to content-neutral speech restrictions:
Speech restrictions survive intermediate scrutiny if they "(a) serve a significant government interest; (b) are narrowly tailored to advance that interest; and (c) leave open ample alternative channels of communication." …
Kansas's stated interests are significant… Kansas identified the harm of voter confusion that the prefilled applications caused. The State says some voters called in angry and perplexed by inaccurate prefilled applications. And it points to others who unnecessarily submitted multiple applications after receiving the prefilled forms. Kansas identified the administrative burdens caused by the erroneously prefilled applications, duplicate submissions (caused, at least in part, by the prefilling confusion), and time spent assuaging voters' concerns and confusion. And Kansas identified lost confidence in the electoral process. County election officials were flooded with calls and letters from voters frustrated by the purported incompetence of their county because of errors in the prefilled applications….
The Prohibition is also adequately tailored to address Kansas's legislative interests and does not restrict substantially more speech than necessary. And because the Prohibition minimally burdens speech, it was not necessary to point to alternative regulatory schemes.
First, minimizing voter confusion. Kansas cites evidence of voter confusion caused by the prefilled applications. Kansas showed that the prefilled applications caused confusion among voters because of the applications' errors and many voters' beliefs that they needed to sign and mail prefilled applications even if they had already submitted one.
The Prohibition is tailored to alleviate this harm. Because of the Prohibition, voters will receive blank ballot applications with no error, removing any confusion resulting when voters received erroneous applications but had previously reported their information change to the county election office. And we can reasonably infer that some voters who felt compelled to submit the prefilled applications will not feel compelled to do the same when they are blank….
[T]he evidence here directly relates to the Prohibition—county officials testified to voter confusion resulting from (1) error in prefilled applications, and (2) receipt of prefilled applications, when voters had already submitted applications….
The Prohibition also does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to minimize voter confusion resulting from prefilled ballot applications. Kansas's solution—outright prohibiting the prefilling of applications—was reasonable and "the threat to free speech posed by the Prohibition is sufficiently small." There are few (if any) less-burdensome alternatives that could cure the problem because "the use of forms by the government inherently requires content restrictions." This showing is sufficient to survive narrow tailoring….
Second, administering efficient elections. Kansas presented evidence of the administrative burden caused by the erroneously prefilled applications (and duplicate submissions of prefilled applications). Kansas demonstrated that county offices regularly received erroneous prefilled applications and duplicate applications because voters believed they needed to submit the prefilled applications they received. Kansas produced evidence that these erroneous prefilled ballots and duplicate submissions produced a significant administrative burden. The three to five minutes processing time for an accurate, non-duplicate application could increase to over thirty minutes. The Prohibition alleviates this processing burden by reducing the amount of erroneously prefilled and duplicate applications county offices receive.
VPC nevertheless counters that Kansas failed to provide evidence of harm because it did not show how many duplicate or inaccurate prefilled applications county offices received. But the record demonstrates that at least 3% of VPC's Kansas voter database was inaccurate, suggesting that VPC sent more than 15,000 erroneous applications to Kansans during the 2020 general election. And county offices reported, without providing exact numbers, that the number of duplicate and erroneous prefilled applications skyrocketed. Kansas offers sufficient evidence supporting the claim that prefilled applications caused administrative harm.
To rebut Kansas's showing of narrow tailoring, VPC also relies on the district court's conclusion that the "real issue" producing the administrative burden was duplicate applications. But Kansas shows that it expended extra resources on duplicates and error-riddled prefilled applications. And Kansas points to evidence showing that voters submitted duplicates in part because they were prefilled—they thought they had to.
The district court reached the contrary conclusion that the prefilled applications did not cause administrative harm in large part because Cox and Shew testified that in some ways they preferred prefilled applications. But the district court erred in concluding that the Prohibition's potential allowance of one problem—increased human error in applications—negated the adequacy of the Prohibition's tailoring to a different problem, third-party error in the prefilled applications. Kansas has a right to act prophylactically to minimize administrative burden, and to do so in its best judgment by addressing one problem contributing to it.
Perhaps the Prohibition will be net neutral. But Kansas tailored the Prohibition to a discrete problem producing an administrative burden and directly ameliorated that problem. And because the Prohibition does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to further Kansas's interest in facilitating efficient elections, the Prohibition is narrowly tailored.
Third, fostering confidence in election integrity. Kansas offers record evidence of voter frustration and distrust caused by the prefilled ballot applications. Howell described voters venting frustration at the alleged incompetence of their county upon receiving applications that contained a wrong name and address; some who had previously communicated changes to the office were especially frustrated. The Prohibition addresses this distrust and frustration by removing the source of the voters' complaints….
Finally, the Prohibition leaves open ample alternative channels of communication. VPC "remains free to choose what avenue of communication it will use to advocate for mail voting, including the use of unsolicited mailers." It may even include a sheet with the previously prefilled information alongside a blank application….
Because the Prohibition is adequately tailored under intermediate scrutiny, its minimal restriction on the content of VPC's speech is permissible under the First Amendment.
Bradley J. Schlozman, Scott R. Schillings and Garrett R. Roe (Hinkle Law Firm LLC) represent defendants.

It urges that the Prohibition functions to target only mail-in voting advocates because those against mail-in voting would not prefill applications.

That may be true, but caselaw forecloses VPC's argument. Without more, incidental disproportionate effect on one subject or viewpoint does not prove improper purpose. See McCullen (majority opinion) ("[A] facially neutral law does not become content based simply because it may disproportionately affect speech on certain topics.")….

VPC fails to show that Kansas enacted the Prohibition to suppress its pro-mail-voting viewpoint. The district court's reliance on cultural antagonism against mail-in voting to infer the Kansas legislature enacted the prohibition with an improper purpose—when the law's justifications, text, and enactment history reveal no such purpose—was in error….

And the court held that the law passed the intermediate scrutiny applicable to content-neutral speech restrictions:

Speech restrictions survive intermediate scrutiny if they "(a) serve a significant government interest; (b) are narrowly tailored to advance that interest; and (c) leave open ample alternative channels of communication." …

Kansas's stated interests are significant… Kansas identified the harm of voter confusion that the prefilled applications caused. The State says some voters called in angry and perplexed by inaccurate prefilled applications. And it points to others who unnecessarily submitted multiple applications after receiving the prefilled forms. Kansas identified the administrative burdens caused by the erroneously prefilled applications, duplicate submissions (caused, at least in part, by the prefilling confusion), and time spent assuaging voters' concerns and confusion. And Kansas identified lost confidence in the electoral process. County election officials were flooded with calls and letters from voters frustrated by the purported incompetence of their county because of errors in the prefilled applications….

The Prohibition is also adequately tailored to address Kansas's legislative interests and does not restrict substantially more speech than necessary. And because the Prohibition minimally burdens speech, it was not necessary to point to alternative regulatory schemes.

First, minimizing voter confusion. Kansas cites evidence of voter confusion caused by the prefilled applications. Kansas showed that the prefilled applications caused confusion among voters because of the applications' errors and many voters' beliefs that they needed to sign and mail prefilled applications even if they had already submitted one.

The Prohibition is tailored to alleviate this harm. Because of the Prohibition, voters will receive blank ballot applications with no error, removing any confusion resulting when voters received erroneous applications but had previously reported their information change to the county election office. And we can reasonably infer that some voters who felt compelled to submit the prefilled applications will not feel compelled to do the same when they are blank….

[T]he evidence here directly relates to the Prohibition—county officials testified to voter confusion resulting from (1) error in prefilled applications, and (2) receipt of prefilled applications, when voters had already submitted applications….

The Prohibition also does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to minimize voter confusion resulting from prefilled ballot applications. Kansas's solution—outright prohibiting the prefilling of applications—was reasonable and "the threat to free speech posed by the Prohibition is sufficiently small." There are few (if any) less-burdensome alternatives that could cure the problem because "the use of forms by the government inherently requires content restrictions." This showing is sufficient to survive narrow tailoring….

Second, administering efficient elections. Kansas presented evidence of the administrative burden caused by the erroneously prefilled applications (and duplicate submissions of prefilled applications). Kansas demonstrated that county offices regularly received erroneous prefilled applications and duplicate applications because voters believed they needed to submit the prefilled applications they received. Kansas produced evidence that these erroneous prefilled ballots and duplicate submissions produced a significant administrative burden. The three to five minutes processing time for an accurate, non-duplicate application could increase to over thirty minutes. The Prohibition alleviates this processing burden by reducing the amount of erroneously prefilled and duplicate applications county offices receive.

VPC nevertheless counters that Kansas failed to provide evidence of harm because it did not show how many duplicate or inaccurate prefilled applications county offices received. But the record demonstrates that at least 3% of VPC's Kansas voter database was inaccurate, suggesting that VPC sent more than 15,000 erroneous applications to Kansans during the 2020 general election. And county offices reported, without providing exact numbers, that the number of duplicate and erroneous prefilled applications skyrocketed. Kansas offers sufficient evidence supporting the claim that prefilled applications caused administrative harm.

To rebut Kansas's showing of narrow tailoring, VPC also relies on the district court's conclusion that the "real issue" producing the administrative burden was duplicate applications. But Kansas shows that it expended extra resources on duplicates and error-riddled prefilled applications. And Kansas points to evidence showing that voters submitted duplicates in part because they were prefilled—they thought they had to.

The district court reached the contrary conclusion that the prefilled applications did not cause administrative harm in large part because Cox and Shew testified that in some ways they preferred prefilled applications. But the district court erred in concluding that the Prohibition's potential allowance of one problem—increased human error in applications—negated the adequacy of the Prohibition's tailoring to a different problem, third-party error in the prefilled applications. Kansas has a right to act prophylactically to minimize administrative burden, and to do so in its best judgment by addressing one problem contributing to it.

Perhaps the Prohibition will be net neutral. But Kansas tailored the Prohibition to a discrete problem producing an administrative burden and directly ameliorated that problem. And because the Prohibition does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to further Kansas's interest in facilitating efficient elections, the Prohibition is narrowly tailored.

Third, fostering confidence in election integrity. Kansas offers record evidence of voter frustration and distrust caused by the prefilled ballot applications. Howell described voters venting frustration at the alleged incompetence of their county upon receiving applications that contained a wrong name and address; some who had previously communicated changes to the office were especially frustrated. The Prohibition addresses this distrust and frustration by removing the source of the voters' complaints….

Finally, the Prohibition leaves open ample alternative channels of communication. VPC "remains free to choose what avenue of communication it will use to advocate for mail voting, including the use of unsolicited mailers." It may even include a sheet with the previously prefilled information alongside a blank application….

Because the Prohibition is adequately tailored under intermediate scrutiny, its minimal restriction on the content of VPC's speech is permissible under the First Amendment.

Bradley J. Schlozman, Scott R. Schillings and Garrett R. Roe (Hinkle Law Firm LLC) represent defendants.

The post Kansas Ban on Private Parties' Partially Prefilling Voters' Mail Ballot Applications Upheld appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Florida "Addictive Features" Social Media Restrictions on Minors Likely Constitutional, Eleventh Circuit Holds
articles.content:
Some short excerpts from the long opinion in Computer & Comm. Indus. Ass'n v. Uthmeier, decided today by Judge Kevin Newsom, joined by Judges Robert Luck and Gerald Bard Tjoflat:
One of the most pressing is how and in what ways social-media use affects minors. According to the State of Florida, social-media companies seed their platforms with "addictive features"—push notifications, auto-play, infinite scrolling, etc.—in order to make them, well, addictive. These features, the state says, are "psychological hooks" that "overstimulate the reward center in the brain" and "foster compulsive overuse." Florida insists that children are particularly susceptible to these "addictive features" because their brains are still developing. In particular, the state contends, the features contribute to "[c]ompulsive or uncontrollable" social-media use among children and threaten a "youth mental health crisis." Children face "'sleep problems, attention problems, and feelings of exclusion,' all of which put [them] at risk of 'depression, anxiety, and neuroticism.'"
In an effort to protect children from social-media addiction and its ensuing effects, Florida passed HB3, which imposes age-restriction requirements on platforms that use "addictive features." In particular, HB3 requires platforms within its ambit to prohibit anyone under the age of 14 from creating an account, and to prohibit anyone else under 16 from doing so without parental consent….
[W]e hold that HB3 likely passes First Amendment muster because it is a content-neutral speech regulation that satisfies intermediate scrutiny….
The court held that HB3 was a speech restriction and thus implicated the First Amendment:
Florida contends that HB3 "regulates product design, not children's speech," and, accordingly, doesn't even implicate the First Amendment. In particular, the state says, HB3 restricts only the creation of accounts, not social-media access writ large, and thus regulates only "commercial transaction[s]"—namely, a platform's ability to "enter[ ] into a contract" with children of a certain age.
Even accepting the state's characterization, it seems clear enough to us that HB3 "disproportionate[ly] burden[s]" CCIA's member platforms' "protected First Amendment activities"—namely, "compiling and curating others' speech" for their users. In particular, HB3 burdens platforms' ability to communicate with their users by requiring them (1) to prohibit minors under 14 years of age from creating or maintaining accounts and (2) to secure parental consent before communicating with 14- and 15-year-olds.
But it concluded that HB3 was content-neutral:
HB3 is facially content neutral: It regulates social-media platforms based on their functional capabilities and features, not the content they communicate. The law neither references the substance of the speech on any platform nor draws distinctions based on it. Put differently, HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them. Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3 so long as (1) a proportion of minors under 16 spend an average of at least two hours a day on it; (2) it uses infinite scrolling, push notifications, auto-play, or livestreaming, or displays user-engagement metrics; and (3) it selects content algorithmically for users. And tellingly, neither a platform nor a user can "avoid or mitigate" the effects of HB3 by "altering" the substance of any posted expression.
HB3's justification is also content neutral: to "protect[ ] children from [social-media] addiction and associated mental-health harms." That purpose is "unrelated to the content of expression" on any given platform, and it doesn't "reflect[ ] disagreement with the message such speech conveys." …
CCIA contends that HB3 is content based because it applies only to so-called "social" speech: The law, CCIA asserts, targets websites "based on the 'social' subject matter 'of the material they disseminate.'" … [But t]he "social"-ness of speech is a function of its form, not its substance. Put simply, "social" speech, as CCIA seems to be using the term, is simply speech that occurs between users on social-media platforms, wholly without regard to "the topic discussed or the idea or message expressed." Users can engage in so-called "social" speech about any topic, from the sublime (religion, philosophy, etc.) to the ridiculous (celebrity gossip, cat videos, etc.)….
And it held that HB3 likely passed the "intermediate scrutiny" applicable to content-neutral speech restrictions, because the law "advances important governmental interests unrelated to the suppression of free speech and does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to further those interests":
CCIA doesn't dispute that HB3 advances an important state interest; it acknowledges that "protecting minors is certainly a laudable goal." Even so, it says, HB3 fails intermediate scrutiny's first element because Florida's interest "is plainly related to the suppression of expression." In particular, CCIA emphasizes that HB3 prohibits addictive features only on websites, not on other "services that disseminate speech"—like, for instance, "books that end in cliffhangers." Florida singles out social-media platforms, CCIA insists, because they host speech that Florida "distrusts."
CCIA's argument doesn't necessarily follow. It would hold up only if websites have an inherent expressive value that differs from the expressive value inherent in all books. But both books and websites communicate content that spans the full range of expressive values; they just do so in different formats. Absent a restriction on the substance of the topics, ideas, or messages communicated by websites as compared to those communicated by books, HB3's "singling out" of websites is not, as CCIA argues, "plainly related to the suppression of expression." …
HB3 [is] also likely … appropriately tailored to advancing Florida's interest in protecting minors. In particular, HB3 doesn't "burden substantially more speech than necessary" because it (1) calibrates its restrictions by age, (2) regulates minors' creation of social-media accounts, not necessarily their access to the platforms themselves, (3) covers only those platforms that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and (4) applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.
First, HB3 is age delimited. It prohibits minors under 14 from creating accounts, and it requires 14- and 15-year-olds to obtain parental consent before doing so. Notably, it imposes no limitations for those 16 years of age and older. The law thus applies only to younger minors and recognizes the fine-grained distinctions even among those to whom it applies—namely, that 13-year-olds (in general, middleschoolers) are different from 14- and 15-year-olds (those starting high school), who, in turn, are different from those 16 and up (budding adults).
Second, even among those to whom HB3 does apply, the law restricts only their ability to create their own accounts, not their ability to access social-media platforms per se. The creation of a social-media account is a commercial act—a business transaction. Even a minor—indeed, even a young child—may continue to use the platforms provided he either (1) uses his parents' (or someone else's) account or (2) gains access without an account.
Third, HB3 targets only the platforms to which many minors are already addicted. As a reminder, a platform comes within HB3's purview only if at least 10% of daily active users under 16 years old spend an average of two hours or more per day on it. Together with its other limitations, HB3's tailoring efforts fall within the broad range of potential legislative solutions that intermediate scrutiny permits.
And fourth, HB3 operates not as an outright prohibition of platform usage but rather as a "conditional ban" of sorts—namely, on platforms' use of addictive features and algorithms. The law applies only to platforms that use a combination of algorithms and addictive features and that succeed in keeping many minors on them for an average of at least two hours a day. Refraining from using either algorithms or addictive features, or remaining below the temporal threshold, exempts a platform from the law's application.
Now, none of that is necessarily to say that HB3 embodies the best policy choice. Maybe, maybe not. But intermediate scrutiny affords governments "latitude … to design regulatory solutions to address content-neutral interests." Accordingly, it is within Florida's discretion to draw the lines it has—many of which, of course, narrow the law's scope. So, for instance, Florida may validly opt to prohibit minors under 14, rather than 16, from creating social-media accounts, and to require 16-year-olds, rather than all those under 18, to obtain their parents' consent before creating accounts. So too, it may validly train its attention on platforms that a segment of children use more than two hours per day, rather than one. And finally, it is free to focus on sites that use both algorithms and "addictive features," rather than one or the other of those….
Judge Newsom also added a very interesting separate opinion, focused on as-applied challenges and intermediate scrutiny; interested readers may want to look at it, as well as at the panel's discussion of overbreadth challenges and other matters.
The post Florida "Addictive Features" Social Media Restrictions on Minors Likely Constitutional, Eleventh Circuit Holds appeared first on Reason Magazine.
